tier_reason: The page (implementation/versusc.md, rendered as docs/implementation/versusc.html) prints both benchmark programs (lineending.bqn and lineending.c), the exact C build line 'clang -O3 -march=native lineending.c' with clang 15.0.7, the CBQN commit 0d2631a2 with its Singeli build options, and the CPU (Tiger Lake i5-1135G7); every quoted ns/elt figure matches. CBQN's makefile at that commit builds with -O3 by default; only the C compiler used to build CBQN itself is unstated, which is how other interpreter entries held at A were treated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Page text: BQN breaks even with C at a little under 200 bytes and hits 5x C's speed on inputs of a few thousand bytes or more with AVX-512 disabled, over 10x with AVX-512 until cache becomes a bottleneck. Page timings on a Tiger Lake i5-1135G7 (a CRLF every ~100 bytes): C (clang 15.0.7 -O3 -march=native) 0.555 ns/elt from 10k to 1M bytes (0.613 at 100 bytes); CBQN avx2/bmi2/pclmul build 0.893 (100 bytes, slower than C), 0.127 (3k), 0.106 (10k), 0.094 (30k), 0.107 (1M) ns/elt, about 4.4x at 3k and 5.2-5.9x from 10k up (derived from page data); CBQN native build (AVX-512) 0.0526 (10k), 0.0506 (30k), 0.0537 (100k), 0.0787 (1M) ns/elt, about 10.3-11.0x from 10k to 300k and 7.1x at 1M (derived from page data). The page's selection figures (0.04 ns per selection from a table of 32 or fewer 1-byte values via shuffles versus 0.2 ns via gather) are two CBQN code paths, not a C measurement. The compiler benchmark (implementation/bootbench.md) is a separate claim: boot3.bqn in CBQN compiles boot2.bqn in 270.6 us versus 415.5 us for dzaima's comp.c built with clang 15.0 (system values and error handling removed), average of 10,000 runs on a Skylake i5-6200U, i.e. 35% less time (about 1.54x, derived from page data); the two compilers use different algorithms and the C build flags are not stated.
corrections.caveats: First-party measurement by the BQN author on one machine; both programs, the C compile line and the CBQN commit and build options are on the page, so it is reproducible (CBQN builds at -O3 with the system cc by default; the compiler used for CBQN is not named). The C baseline is the plain portable scalar loop the author took from his 2017 Dyalog talk; clang 15 makes it branchless and unrolls it 4x, so it is not crippled, but no SIMD-intrinsic or memchr/memcpy-chunk C version was tested and the page says specialized C is always faster. The win is CBQN's hand-written Singeli SIMD Replicate primitive (an adaptive sparse/dense compress) against compiler output for a scalar loop: a best case for BQN primitives, as the page itself says ('combinations of primitives never do so well'); density 1/100 is described as not particularly favourable. Not the same algorithm in the strict sense (data-parallel mask plus Replicate versus a sequential scan), but output is identical. The selection figures (0.04 versus 0.2 ns) compare two CBQN paths, not C. The compiler benchmark side claim (35% faster) ran on different hardware (i5-6200U), compares different compiler designs and states no C flags. The page dates from 2023 (clang 15.0.7, gcc 12.2.1; 'the C compilers of today (2023)') and CBQN has changed since. Licence: most files LGPL-3.0-only OR GPL-3.0-only OR MPL-2.0 at the user's choice; timsort files MIT and Ryu Apache-2.0 or BSL-1.0.

notes: All numbers match the page; native-build ratio corrected to 7.1-11.0x and the selection figure reclassified as CBQN-internal (both paths are CBQN). Shortcomings to record: first-party single-machine 2023 run; C side is portable scalar code at -O3 -march=native (no intrinsics or memchr-based version), so the win is CBQN's SIMD Replicate primitive and a best case by the author's own account; compiler-benchmark side claim on other hardware with different algorithms and unstated C flags. CBQN is not listed in any earlier wave.

tier_reason: The kostya/benchmarks README (UPDATE 2026-07-19, Xeon E-2324G, versions listed) shows D/gdc 1.505 s, D/ldc2 1.722 s, D/dmd 1.880 s against C/gcc 3.034 s and C/clang 3.067 s, with code (matmul/matmul.c, matmul/matmul.d) and flags (common/commands.mk) public, so the harness is A-grade; capped at C because the comparison is not like for like: matmul.d calls Phobos std.numeric.dotProduct, a hand-unrolled 16-wide kernel with two partial sums, against a single-accumulator strict-FP C loop, and the like-for-like D port in attractivechaos/plb2 (same i-k-j loop in D and C) is slower than C (ldc2 0.57 s versus clang 0.54 s on Apple M1), so the 2x is a kernel difference, not a D advantage (asymmetric-comparison precedent, as TensorFlow and GStreamer B to C).

corrections.claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks matmul table (median, Xeon E-2324G, README updated 2026-07-19): D/gdc 1.505 s, D/ldc2 1.722 s, D/dmd 1.880 s versus C/gcc 3.034 s and C/clang 3.067 s, i.e. gdc about 2.0x, ldc2 about 1.76x and dmd about 1.61x faster than gcc C (derived from page data). Rust 3.067 s, Zig 3.071 s and Nim/gcc 3.091 s tie with C. Not like for like: the D program calls std.numeric.dotProduct (two partial sums) while every tied language runs the single-accumulator loop; in the like-for-like plb2 matmul (same i-k-j loop in D and C, Apple M1) D ldc2 1.35.0 takes 0.57 s versus C clang 15.0.0 0.54 s, so D is about 5% slower there (derived from page data). BLAS-backed rows (D lubeck 0.042 s, C++ Eigen 0.081 s, NumPy, Arraymancer) are library comparisons and excluded.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: From common/commands.mk: C gcc 16.1.0 / clang 22.1.8 '-Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -std=c23'; D ldc2 1.41.0 '-O5 -release -boundscheck=off', gdc 14.2.0 '-O3 -frelease -finline -fbounds-check=off', dmd v2.111.0 '-O -release -inline -boundscheck=off'. The D builds carry no -march=native and no LTO, so the flag difference favours C.
corrections.why_faster: Confirmed from Phobos source (std/numeric.d, dotProduct(F1, F2)(in F1[], in F2[])): the array overload unrolls 16 elements per iteration into two partial sums (sum0, sum1) plus a 4-wide block and a scalar tail, so two independent floating-point add chains run in parallel; the C loop keeps one accumulator and, without -ffast-math, the compiler may not reassociate it, so it is bound by FP add latency. The about 2x gap matches the two chains (inference). This is a standard-library kernel and reduction-order difference, not codegen: the same two-accumulator loop in portable C would recover it, and like-for-like D is slightly slower than C in plb2.
corrections.caveats: Not a language or compiler advantage: the high-level algorithm (transpose plus dot products) is the same, but the timed D path is Phobos' hand-unrolled two-accumulator dotProduct against a naive single-accumulator C loop, so summation order and results differ in the last bits (the harness only checks within 0.1 at n=101). Like for like (plb2, same loop in both languages) D ldc2 is slower than C. The C row is deliberately plain ('written as the average developer would'); C gets -march=native and -flto=auto that the D builds lack. gcc 16.1 and clang 22 are newer than the GCC 14 and LLVM bases of gdc and ldc2. Time includes allocation (D uses GC-allocated jagged arrays, C malloc/calloc rows) and matrix generation.

notes: Numbers match the README row for row and the flags match common/commands.mk. Shortcoming to record: the 2x comes from std.numeric.dotProduct's two partial sums (different accumulator structure and FP order) against a single-accumulator C loop; like-for-like plb2 shows D ldc2 0.57 s slower than C 0.54 s, so it is not a D language win. Held at C rather than D because the C build is fully optimised (-O3 -march=native -flto) and both programs follow the suite's common reference implementation; the orchestrator may treat the tuned library kernel as the crippled-baseline case if it prefers.

tier_reason: Raised from B: the plb2 README appendix table (Apple M1 MacBook Pro, hyperfine) shows f90:gcc 13.2.0 matmul 0.51 s and c:clang 15.0.0 0.54 s, and the code (src/fortran/matmul.F90, src/c/matmul.c), flags (src/fortran/Makefile FFLAGS=-O3, src/c/Makefile CFLAGS=-O3 -fwrapv -flto), compiler versions and CPU model are all public, which meets A for an independent suite (as kostya-based entries in wave 12). The margin itself is small; see caveats.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Fortran: gfortran 13.2.0 with FFLAGS=-O3 (src/fortran/Makefile); C: clang 15.0.0 via $(CC) with CFLAGS=-O3 -fwrapv -flto (src/c/Makefile). Neither side passes -march/-mcpu.
corrections.workload: Multiply two 1500x1500 double-precision matrices with triple-nested loops (no BLAS), one of four plb2 tasks. C (src/c/matmul.c) uses row pointers into one contiguous calloc block with i-k-j order (inner loop over j, c[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j]); Fortran (src/fortran/matmul.F90) uses column-major explicit-shape dummy arrays with j-k-i order (inner loop over i), the same unit-stride access pattern and the same work. Elapsed wall time includes matrix generation and process startup.
corrections.why_faster: Not stated by the source and not confirmed. Plausible factors: Fortran explicit-shape dummy arrays are contiguous and may not alias, so gfortran needs no runtime overlap checks, while the C version writes through double** row pointers; but the compilers also differ (GCC 13 backend versus clang 15/LLVM), so the 6% may be backend codegen rather than a language property.
corrections.caveats: Margin is about 6% (0.51 s versus 0.54 s) on one machine, single figures without variance in the table, and the rows were timed on different days (Fortran timing added 2024-01-04 as plb2 grew through January 2024), so this is a near-tie that may sit within run-to-run noise. Different compiler backends (gfortran versus clang), so the language and the compiler are confounded; no gcc-built C row exists. Both sides are at -O3 and neither uses -march; the C side adds -fwrapv and -flto (no effect expected on a one-file program). Fortran is the only language in the table that beats C on matmul; the README notes Clang already hoists the inner-loop invariants that many other languages cannot. Elapsed wall time includes process startup. CC0-1.0 dedication: no patent grant. Repository last changed 2025-01-30.

notes: Numbers match the README table; sources and Makefiles confirm the same algorithm and work on both sides (i-k-j row-major versus j-k-i column-major). same_opt_level corrected to true (both -O3, neither -march; the record wrongly implied C had -march). Shortcomings to record: about 6% near-tie on one M1 with rows timed on different days, gfortran versus clang confounds language with compiler backend, mechanism unconfirmed, CC0 has no patent grant.
